content: Stimulus control refers to the phenomenon where the presence of a specific stimulus increases the likelihood of a particular behavior occurring. This occurs because the behavior has been reinforced in the past when that stimulus was present. Essentially, stimulus control involves learning to recognize environmental cues, known as discriminative stimuli, that provide information about whether a behavior will be effective or ineffective, under what conditions, and what consequences (reinforcement or punishment) the behavior will produce. As a result, individuals or animals are more likely to respond differently depending on the presence or absence of these stimuli. To illustrate this concept, consider an experiment involving a pigeon. The pigeon is initially trained to peck a left key to receive food as a reinforcer. Once the pigeon learns this task, a right key is illuminated with a red light. At first, the red light on the right key does not provide meaningful information to the pigeon, so it is eventually ignored. However, if the procedure is modified such that food is only provided when the pigeon pecks the left key while the right key is illuminated, the pigeon begins to associate the illuminated right key with the opportunity to obtain food. Consequently, the pigeon starts pecking the left key only when the right key is lit and not when it is dark. This demonstrates that the pigeon’s behavior is now under the control of the discriminative stimulus (the illuminated right key). It is important to note that control in this context does not imply that the pigeon lacks free will or choice. Instead, it refers to the increased probability of a specific response occurring in the presence of the discriminative stimulus. The opposite of discrimination, where an individual learns to respond to one stimulus but not another (e.g., the pigeon pecks the left key only when the right key is illuminated), is known as generalization. Generalization occurs when an individual exhibits similar behavior in response to stimuli that are similar to the original discriminative stimulus. For example, after the pigeon has learned to peck the left key only when the right key is illuminated with a specific red light, what would happen if the intensity or wavelength of the red light is altered? To investigate this, researchers could present five variations of the red light, each for a brief period (e.g. The typical result, observed across various species including pigeons, rats, monkeys, goldfish, and even humans, is that the highest response rate occurs with the original training stimulus (the initial red light). The response rate then systematically decreases as the physical difference between the training stimulus and the test stimuli increases. In the field of Quantitative Analysis of Behavior, stimulus control is studied through various methods, including Matching-to-Sample and signal detection. Matching-to-Sample is a type of conditional discrimination procedure. In this procedure, one of two or more comparison stimuli presented shares a specific property (e.g., shape) with a sample stimulus. Responses to the matching stimulus are reinforced. A variation of this procedure, known as Oddity Matching, involves reinforcing responses to the comparison stimulus that does not match the sample. For further exploration of these concepts, see topics such as Signal Detection and Quantitative Analysis of Behavior.
